title: Good Shepherd Sunday
hook: the fourth Sunday of Easter, a day of prayer for vocations

segments.voice: Yesterday, Divine Mercy Sunday and misericordia. Your line was Jesus, I trust in you.

Somebody calls your name across a crowded airport. You turn before you've even thought about it, not because the voice was loud, but because it was yours. Two Sundays after the octave ends, on the fourth Sunday of Easter, every Catholic parish in the world hears a Gospel about exactly that: a shepherd whose sheep know his voice. And since 1964 the Church has made it a day of prayer about a call.
screen: `A NAME ACROSS AN AIRPORT.` → `THE FOURTH SUNDAY OF EASTER.` → `A DAY ABOUT A CALL.`

segments.voice: Every year on this Sunday the Gospel comes from John chapter ten, a different slice of it in each year of the three-year cycle. In one year, the gate of the sheepfold, and this line, in the Douay-Rheims: "the sheep hear his voice: and he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out." In another, I am the good shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep. In the third, my sheep hear my voice, and no one shall snatch them out of my hand. A shepherd in Jesus's world didn't drive his flock from behind with dogs. He walked ahead and called, and they followed the voice they knew. The word vocation comes from the Latin vocare, to call. In 1964 Pope Paul VI began a World Day of Prayer for Vocations, and it settled on this Sunday. Most parishes pray especially for priests and for men and women entering religious life, and you'll often hear a seminarian or a sister speak at Mass. But the Church uses the word more widely than that. The Catechism speaks of a vocation to love that everyone has, and of marriage as a vocation too. A married couple, a single person caring for a parent, a nurse on night shifts: Catholic teaching says each of them can be answering a call. And the call in John isn't a job description first. It's a name. He calls his own by name, and then leads them out.
screen: `JOHN TEN, EVERY YEAR.` · `A SHEPHERD WALKS AHEAD AND CALLS.` · `VOCARE: TO CALL.` · `PRIESTS, SISTERS, MARRIAGE, EVERYONE.` · then, large: `HE CALLETH HIS OWN SHEEP BY NAME.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you know who is at a fork right now: a young person wondering about the priesthood or the convent, a friend deciding whether to marry, change careers, or move home to care for someone. Picture their face and say their name quietly. If you pray, you can pray for them by name; if you don't, simply wish them clarity and courage.
Vocation. From the Latin vocare, to call. In Catholic teaching, a call from God, to priesthood, religious life, marriage, or a life of love in the world. Today's word.
Your line: he calls by name. Nobody is called as a number. Day six hundred sixty-seven, done.
